newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmiri militants suspected in India train blast.
newsitem.headline: Kashmiri militants suspected in India train blast.

text.p: Indian investigators said on Tuesday they believed Kashmiri, not Sikh, militants planted a bomb on a train which killed 12 people.

Twelve passengers were killed and 37 injured early on Monday by the explosion, which shattered a sleeper coach at Ambala cantonment station near Chandigarh, capital of the northern state of Punjab. No one has claimed responsibility.

The blast roused fears of a renewal of Sikh separatist violence in the Punjab region before local elections due by February. It prompted a security crackdown, including stepped up sweeps on hideouts of suspected Sikh militants.
But police investigating the attack said they now doubted Sikh militants fighting for a separate homeland were responsible.
"It appears to be an act of terrorist violence involving Kashmiri militants," a senior police official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters in Chandigarh.

"I say so because Kashmiri militants never own responsibility for such blasts," the official said. "Past experience shows that Sikh militants had been claiming responsibility for such incidents within half an hour."
The Press Trust of India also said investigators suspected Kashmiri militants were behind the explosion.
The train was headed for Jammu city, winter capital of troubled Jammu and Kashmir state, which borders Punjab to the north.

More than 20,000 people have died since a separatist revolt erupted in the Himalayan state in 1990. Similar numbers of people are estimated to have died in the Punjab rebellion, which lasted for a decade until the early 1990s.
Police said on Tuesday that they had issued a "red alert", ordering officers to step up surveillance of all vehicles, trains and buses in the Punjab region.
"We have stepped up security in the state and we are not taking any chances," Punjab Chief Minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal said.
"All security precautions are being strictly taken at public places, including railways stations and bus stands," he said.

Chandigarh police chief Manoj Yadav said authorities were concentrating on vehicles coming into the city. "We are searching buses and trains besides all private vehicles. On suspicion, we also check the luggage," he said.
Railways Minister Ram Vilas Paswan told parliament on Tuesday that authorities had intensified checks at all railway stations, using sniffer dogs where possible.
The blast was the deadliest attack on a train in the region since Sikh militants stopped a train near Ludhiana city in late 1991 and slaughtered at least 53 passengers, most of whom were Hindus.

Police intelligence officials told Reuters they recently circulated a warning that Sikh militants had crossed into Punjab state from neighbouring Pakistan and were preparing to launch an attack in early December.
